Saliba explains this partly through the influence of the political life of Ibn Sīnā’s time. In his view, the image of “God” in Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics reflects the position of the Abbasid caliph after the central authority of the caliphate had broken down into principalities and smaller states with a wide degree of independence:

“The caliph remained in Baghdad without knowing what the sultans were doing in their different kingdoms. The caliph was therefore the One who does not move, the absolute Good that cannot be reached, and the First Principle toward which the intellects turn. The princes and sultans were intellects independent of him yet connected to him, because they shared in what he brought into being and received goodness from him.

“In Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics, every planet is a king moving through the heavens in praise of God, just as the sultans and princes move in the service of the caliph who remains in Baghdad. Heaven became a state in which the directing power was separated from the power that sets things in motion, while political life was organized in the image of the celestial spheres and their movements.
“Ibn Sīnā’s ideas, then, are not visions sent down from heaven. They are confused dreams filled with the vapors of the earth.”
This is a genuinely historical insight. It connects Ibn Sīnā’s intellectual work closely and precisely with the social and political world in which he lived.
Yet the same researcher falls back into the “ahistorical” method in some of his other analyses.

Take his comparison between al-Fārābī’s “city” and Plato’s Republic. Saliba rightly notices the many differences between them. One of the most important is the difference between al-Fārābī’s idea of society, which embraces all the peoples of the earth and which he considers the highest form of human society, with the great universal state as the best state through which happiness can be achieved, and Plato’s idea of society, which is confined to a small city such as Athens or Sparta.

Saliba sees this difference. From the standpoint of a scientific approach to history, it is extremely important. Yet instead of asking about its historical roots, he explains it only through “the influence of religious belief”:

“Had he—al-Fārābī—not learned that ‘man is the brother of man, whether he likes it or not’? Had he not learned that ‘an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab except through piety,’ and that piety brings all nations together within a single fold...?”

We are not denying that religion can shape philosophical ideas, especially in a historical period when religion has enormous influence. But even under those conditions, religion cannot be the decisive factor. It is one factor among others, and all those other factors together still do not have the same decisive weight as the social relations that dominate a particular society at a particular stage of its history.
This applies directly to the difference between al-Fārābī’s vision of a large and far-reaching society and Plato’s much narrower vision.

The historical conditions surrounding Plato’s philosophy were those of a slave society. The Greek cities were divided from one another. They formed separate societies that were neither integrated nor closely connected, and they were often at war. They were therefore closed societies.

Intellectual work was largely confined to the class of “masters,” while manual work—the actual process of material production—was confined to the class of “slaves.” Philosophy therefore expressed the outlook of the master class alone.

This helps explain why Plato gave philosophers alone the right to lead the “republic,” and why he reserved philosophy for one section of the “people,” which he regarded as uniquely qualified to govern it.

Although Plato lived under a form of slave-owning democracy, he was an enemy of that democracy. He saw many weaknesses in it and even regarded it as one form of the decline of the state. His Republic and Laws were both a rejection of this form of democracy.

But even the idea of democracy in Plato’s time had an aristocratic, slave-owning character. Democracy was understood as government elected by the class that made up the majority of the recognized political community. The Greek word democracy does indeed mean “rule of the people,” but “the people” meant the free citizens—the class that held political power—not the slaves.
In Plato’s teaching, the state, or republic, does not change or develop. It resembles his eternal Forms: fixed and incapable of change.
His division of society into classes was also based not on production, but on consumption.

In short, Plato lived at a time when the Athenian city-state—the state of slave-owning democracy—was in decline. When he condemned “democracy,” understood as rule by those seeking power and wealth, and condemned oligarchy—the rule of a minority over the majority—as well as democratic and despotic forms of rule, his thinking reflected the real political condition of the city-state. Slave-owning democracy had lost its earlier substance and much of its political, economic, and military strength.

For all these reasons, Plato’s thought remained within the limits of this particular reality. It revolved around problems confined to the Greek city-state and to the internal struggle among the political and ideological forces that represented its social order.
The historical conditions in which al-Fārābī lived were completely different.

His world was a medieval Arab-Islamic society in which feudal social relations had become firmly established. Its territory stretched across enormous parts of Asia and Africa, as well as parts of Europe. It contained many peoples, regions, and cultures. Political authority was divided among many centers, including rival forms of caliphal authority itself. Across this vast territory ran busy networks of trade and communication.

At the same time, the productive forces were developing in most regions of the state, although at different rates. This encouraged the development of the sciences. Scientific advances helped improve irrigation in agriculture and contributed to the growth of trade and urban crafts.

The interaction between science and material production was accompanied by another kind of interaction: human and cultural contact between the Arabs and their culture on one side, and the other peoples and cultures of the caliphate on the other.

Arabic played a major role in deepening this exchange because it was both the language of the state and the language of Islam. It became a shared means of expressing the results of material and intellectual contact among peoples with very different historical backgrounds. With both its existing strengths and the new capacities it developed, Arabic became something like a main channel into which many different streams of social consciousness flowed.

These historical conditions—in their economic, social, scientific, linguistic, and demographic dimensions—combined with Islam’s rejection of narrow ethnic loyalties to open before al-Fārābī the broad intellectual horizon reflected in his idea of the most complete society: a society embracing all nations within a single state.
2 — Muhammad Uthman Najati examines Ibn Sīnā’s ideas on psychology.

He points out that Ibn Sīnā drew heavily on Aristotle, but also benefited from sources that Aristotle himself could never have used, especially the medical and anatomical studies produced in the centuries after Aristotle.

This helps explain why Ibn Sīnā’s psychology surpasses Aristotle’s in many areas. European historians of philosophy have often treated Aristotle’s psychology—wrongly or at least too loosely—as the only complete model of ancient psychology. In reality, Najati argues, Ibn Sīnā’s psychology is the only genuinely complete model of ancient psychology as a whole.
Najati also notes, however, that Ibn Sīnā’s psychology has important weaknesses. He connects these weaknesses to the limited tools available for research and experiment at the time.

Researchers in Ibn Sīnā’s age had to rely on observation with the naked eye. They did not know the microscope, let alone the many instruments available to scientists today. Their knowledge of the nervous system was therefore incomplete in many respects. For the same reason, they knew very little about the structure of the brain and the sense organs, or about the nature of nervous activity.

This way of looking at the relationship between the development of philosophical thought—psychology was then part of philosophy—and the development of scientific knowledge is another important feature of a scientific approach to history.

Philosophy is relatively independent of the specialized sciences that examine particular parts of the universe. It differs from those sciences because it deals with questions that arise from its own task: the search for the broadest and most general laws.

But this relative independence does not mean that philosophy can develop apart from physics, chemistry, mathematics, the natural sciences, or the human sciences. Philosophy must draw on them, and especially on their latest discoveries, whenever these discoveries help it reach more general conclusions or confirm the validity of those conclusions.

From this point of view, Najati is right to connect both the advances and the weaknesses of Ibn Sīnā’s psychology with the level of scientific and technical knowledge in Ibn Sīnā’s age, just as they were also connected with the social relations of that age.

His study of “Sensory Perception in Ibn Sīnā” is mainly analytical, but it is also a careful specialist study. It is precise, covers its subject thoroughly, and follows the methods of specialized science—in other words, it preserves the kind of objectivity that such sciences can maintain independently of the philosophical commitments of different schools of thought.

This valuable study is far removed from the traditionalist method. Its analysis includes useful comparisons between Ibn Sīnā’s views and judgments on psychological questions and the discoveries of modern science, which have shown some of those older views to be wrong.
One example is Ibn Sīnā’s theory of psychic powers, to which he attributes biological functions such as nutrition, growth, and reproduction. Najati writes:

“Modern science rejects the idea of psychic powers as found in Ibn Sīnā and other ancient psychologists, because such powers cannot be subjected to observation and experiment. A scientific explanation of psychological phenomena requires us to observe them carefully, discover the relationships between them, and derive the laws that connect them, without reducing them to powers that cannot themselves be observed.”
Najati then adds that Ibn Sīnā “did not fail to observe psychological phenomena carefully, but his investigations in this area are often mixed with metaphysical theories.”

Observations of this kind are not unusual in Muhammad Uthman Najati’s presentation of Ibn Sīnā’s psychology. They clearly begin from scientific thinking. They are far removed from the assumptions of positivist philosophy and much closer to a dialectical view of psychological phenomena.

This is therefore one of the contemporary studies that tries to produce modern scientific knowledge about one part of our philosophical heritage without turning the supernatural ideas found in that heritage into doctrines to be preached in the present.
In recent years, however, another change has taken place.

The Arab liberation movement has developed to the point where ideological differences are turning into open ideological conflict. As a result, studies of the intellectual heritage have increasingly begun to state their own starting points openly and to present themselves as weapons in this struggle, on one side or the other.

On the traditionalist side, for example, an Arab journal concerned with studies of this kind devoted one of its issues to important aspects of our intellectual heritage. It explained that it was examining the heritage of “Islamic thought” at this particular moment because this was “one of the most dangerous stages in the history of its development”—meaning the development of the “Islamic world.”

The journal explains this “danger” by saying that the Islamic world is being exposed to many imported Western intellectual trends and ideologies whose novelty and apparent attraction are drawing in many minds.
Speaking in the name of the editors, it declares that “the age in which we live is an age of fierce ideological struggle unlike anything humanity has ever seen before.”
We can see here an ideological position expressed in three main ways.
First, the ideological struggle of our time is redirected away from its actual social basis and given a different meaning.
Second, as a result of this, the heritage is presented as purely religious. Its social and historical content is emptied out, while its national character is obscured.
Third, the journal adopts an increasingly right-wing tone toward progressive ideological movements by describing them as “imported Western” ideologies.
What matters most for us here, however, is the change taking place within the traditionalist camp itself. This change also appears in three ways.

First, traditionalists now state openly and directly that they begin their study of the heritage from an ideological position. In the past, they hid this position behind claims that they simply wanted to “revive the heritage” for its own sake. They would even object to any suggestion that the study of the heritage had anything to do with ideology.
Second, the traditionalist camp now accepts not only that ideological struggle exists, but that in our own time it has reached a level of intensity supposedly unmatched in human history.
Third, its attitude toward “imported Western ideological trends” has changed in a noticeable way.
The same editorial now speaks of the need to:

“probe deeply into these new ideologies and schools of thought, determine Islam’s position toward them, discover what can be accepted and what must be rejected, and find a way to adapt some of these modern trends and intellectual positions and bring them into conformity with Islamic life and institutions, so that they may ultimately—where possible—be absorbed into the framework of authentic Islamic thought. It is also necessary to identify the aspects of the traditional systems and ways of life prevailing in Islamic society itself that can be modified so that they can keep pace and fit with the conditions prevailing in the rest of the world.”

The journal is now speaking of “accepting” some of these “imported Western trends,” where it believes acceptance is possible. It speaks of adapting and subordinating some of them. It even speaks of modifying “the traditional systems and ways of life now prevailing” and making them compatible with conditions in the rest of the world.

This amounts, first, to accepting the need for some positive engagement with progressive intellectual trends, whereas the right-wing traditionalist camp had previously treated them mainly in negative terms.

Second, it amounts to admitting that “the traditional systems and ways of life now prevailing” can no longer remain exactly as they are. They too must undergo change if they are to adjust to the transformations of the modern world.

We describe this as a real change because these statements appeared in an Arab journal issued by an official institution in an Arab state that no one would yet place firmly among the progressive Arab regimes.

We therefore cannot treat them as the isolated personal opinion of a single writer. They should be understood as the expression of an intellectual current created by the conditions of this historical period—objective conditions connected across both the Arab world and the wider world.
On the other, progressive side, studies of different parts of the heritage have increasingly entered the ideological struggle directly.

Some of these studies focus on currents within the heritage that historically represented positions with relatively progressive social and political dimensions for their own time. Muʿtazilite thought, in general, is one of the leading examples.

One such study approaches the Muʿtazila from a contemporary progressive ideological position. It argues that Muʿtazilite thought took up “the question of human freedom and the human standpoint,” and that this question “concerns human beings and their relationship with society and the universe. Because these relationships continue and remain complex—and indeed because their complexity continues to increase—the question itself has remained alive, continuing to generate research and debate down to the present.”

The study argues that examining the Muʿtazilite question today is important for reasons that go far beyond “doing justice to these predecessors and presenting their discussions of the subject.” It is also directly relevant to “the problems of our own age and to the Arab-Muslim human being living in the second half of the twentieth century (...) from an angle of great importance and seriousness for the Arab world in general and for us in Egypt in particular.”

“the need to clarify the thought of this Arab-Islamic school on the question of human freedom; the importance of shedding more light on this subject; and the need to stimulate intellectual debate about the place of this thought in the mind of our nation, in its conduct today, and in the future we seek for it. In short, we must ask what place this thought can have in the intellectual and cultural revolution that is needed if we are to change the intellectual position of our broad masses.”
That is the starting point on which this new study of Muʿtazilite thought is built.

Its method is consistent with that starting point. It follows a scientific historical approach by identifying the political and social dimensions of the issue under study in light of the historical conditions in which that issue originally appeared.
The study also does a good job of explaining the relationship between this inherited material and the ideological reason for studying it in the present.
One of the most important points concerns terminology.

The author notices that the problem of freedom, along with the political and social questions connected with it, was not discussed in the past under the terms “freedom” and “despotism.” It was discussed instead through the concepts of “compulsion” (jabr) and “choice” (ikhtiyār).
In other words, the terminology of the debate changed and developed, just as the scope and content of the debate itself changed and developed.

The author also notes that some researchers—naturally, supporters of traditionalist ideology—have used the difference between past and present terminology to play down the importance of Arab-Muslim discussions of these questions. They have even tried to deny that the Arab-Islamic heritage deserves any credit for examining human freedom at all.

“At no point in Islam was a connection ever established between ‘choice,’ as a theological problem, and ‘freedom’ in general. Nor was choice regarded as one aspect of freedom. It remained a narrow term, stripped of its potential force because of the direction Muslim theologians took in discussing the problem of free will. Human freedom of will was generally reduced to choice in individual situations.”
The author answers that “a difference in the terms used to discuss a question is not a valid reason for concluding that the meanings placed under those terms were also different.”

He supports his answer with many passages from recognized primary and secondary sources, along with examples from Arabic poetry dating back to the age of the Muʿtazila. Together, they show that the meanings carried by the older terms are consistent with the meanings into which those terms later developed in our own age.

Among the writings that follow this new direction and have appeared in recent years, we can also mention a study of Ibn Rushd whose title describes him as “the most controversial figure” and as “a man of thought and action.”
The study succeeds in explaining both descriptions historically.
It begins with the long debate over how Ibn Rushd’s philosophical position should be understood, both in the Arab-Islamic world and in Europe.
Was his philosophy materialist and atheistic, as some philosophers and historians of philosophy have argued?
Was it idealist and rooted in Islamic faith, as another group has claimed?
Or was it a philosophy of compromise, attempting a “reconciliation” between religion and philosophy, as many traditionalist and bourgeois Arab and Muslim researchers have maintained?

The author of this new study does not try to enter the debate openly as one of its direct participants. In practice, however, he does take a side. He does so by uncovering the materialist and progressive elements in the philosophy of the thinker from Córdoba.
These elements place Ibn Rushd in what the author sees as his true historical position: a philosopher for whom

“discussion has an exceptional importance because his thought was joined to the practice of that thought. This involved firm positions against many enemies of the enlightened rational thinking that Ibn Rushd defended, and for which he suffered persecution, rejection, and attacks on his reputation.”
